Dear Stan developers:

I have tried increasing (adapt_delta=0.9999999999,max_treedepth=18,stepsize=0.001) however, it still behaves this way.

Kindest regards,

I'm afraid I don't have time to dig through long
models. Is there some way to use loops to cut down on
the code size? Or to summarize what you're trying to do?
Often, problems arise from hierarchical models with centered
parameterizations and the non-centered approach will fit
much better.

The divergent transitions are just places where Stan has
numerical problems simulating the Hamiltonian. The low
n_eff is more worrying.

I didn't follow the missing data question. Stan doesn't
allow NA data from R, so it all has to be modeled. If
it's a parameter (being estimated), then it's not data.
R-hat will be NaN in cases where all of the draws have the
exact same value.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] general questions regarding divergent transitions after warmup
parts:
Jaslene,

The immediate answer is that the Rhat and ESS codes have trouble with constants, so
you shouldn’t worry about those results.  Ultimately this is because there is a very thin
line between a parameter not moving at all (constant) and a parameter moving very, 
very slowly (large autocorrelations).

Note, however, that when you have missing data trying to simulate the missing values 
doesn’t actually do much.  The problem is that you can never recover the missing 
information, so simulating those values doesn’t improve the fit at all.  It is much more
preferable to marginalize the missing values out of the likelihood, for example

p(d_obs | theta) = \int d(d_missing) p(d_obs, d_missing | theta),

and then fit using the marginalized likelihood.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] general questions regarding divergent transitions after warmup
parts:
I would not advise trusting the posterior.

A divergence indicates that there is some pathological neighborhood in parameter
space that Stan is not able to explore.  That neighborhood might be extremely small,
in which case you could possibly ignore it, or it might be really big, in which case
you absolutely cannot without biasing your fit significantly.

If the pathological neighborhood is small then you should be able to remove the
divergences by decreasing the step size, which is accomplished by increasing
the adapt_depth.  Hence the recommendation in RStan.

But if increasing adapt_delta doesn’t remove the divergences then you have a
large pathological region.  In particular, small increases to adapt_delta let you
explore the neighborhood a bit more, but that just lets you see more pathologies
and hence more divergences pop up.  So the fact that the divergences persist
even as you increase adapt_delta is a sign that there is something seriously
wrong.

If your model is hierarchical then you’ll definitely need the non-centered
parameterization if you’re seeing divergences.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] general questions regarding divergent transitions after warmup
parts:
Again, the concern here is that the divergences persist even for very small step sizes,
which suggests that the pathological neighborhoods are relevant.  Note also that once
you get past adapt_delta = 0.999 or so it becomes harder and harder to get smaller
step sizes by increasing adapt_delta, so there’s not much else you can do with tuning.

Why would these pathologies be relevant even if you don’t always see divergences?
Intuitively, the number of divergences are proportional to the _boundary_ of the pathological
neighborhood, not it’s volume or probability, which determine how strongly ignoring those
neighborhoods might bias your MCMC estimators.

If you see lots of divergences then you have a pathological neighborhood with a large
boundary that suggests large volume/probability and large biases.  This is clearly bad.

If you see occasional divergences then the pathological neighborhood has a small boundary,
and this could mean two things.  First, the neighborhood could just be small and ignoring
it might be okay.  But it could also just be that the neighborhood is elongated and exposes
just a small surface to the sampler even though it has appreciable probability and could
be important for accurate estimators.

The fact that the divergences persist even for small step sizes would suggest the latter
case, which is why I would still be suspicious and continue to try to improve your model
implementation.  In particular, try to identify where in parameter space the divergences
arise to see if you can figure out what correlations might be causing them.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] general questions regarding divergent transitions after warmup
parts:
Is there a way to figure out where the divergences happen?   I only
see displays in RStan of where the initial point is, but the diverging
neighborhood is only indirectly related to these locations.

It’s not the initial point that is shown, but the point sampled from the
trajectory prior to proposing the new subtree with the divergence.
It’s still not exactly where the divergence occurred, but it can be closer 
than the initial point.  Also, a divergence is technically a property of
the trajectory and not a single point, so it can be difficult to track back
and blame a single point even if the entire trajectory was saved.

Can running adaptation longer help?  The reason I ask is that if step
sizes / mass matrix is too big, it'll also cause divergences.

Yes, but it would cause constant divergences, not spurious ones.
Riemannian could help, but in general the mass matrix would have
to be especially poor to cause serious divergence problems.

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] general questions regarding divergent transitions after warmup
parts: Soon we'll be able to recommend that people try RHMC on such models, right?

On Aug 10, 2016, at 12:59 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

Again, the concern here is that the divergences persist even for very small step sizes,
which suggests that the pathological neighborhoods are relevant.  Note also that once
you get past adapt_delta = 0.999 or so it becomes harder and harder to get smaller
step sizes by increasing adapt_delta, so there’s not much else you can do with tuning.

Why would these pathologies be relevant even if you don’t always see divergences?
Intuitively, the number of divergences are proportional to the _boundary_ of the pathological
neighborhood, not it’s volume or probability, which determine how strongly ignoring those
neighborhoods might bias your MCMC estimators.

If you see lots of divergences then you have a pathological neighborhood with a large
boundary that suggests large volume/probability and large biases.  This is clearly bad.

If you see occasional divergences then the pathological neighborhood has a small boundary,
and this could mean two things.  First, the neighborhood could just be small and ignoring
it might be okay.  But it could also just be that the neighborhood is elongated and exposes
just a small surface to the sampler even though it has appreciable probability and could
be important for accurate estimators.

The fact that the divergences persist even for small step sizes would suggest the latter
case, which is why I would still be suspicious and continue to try to improve your model
implementation.  In particular, try to identify where in parameter space the divergences
arise to see if you can figure out what correlations might be causing them.


On Aug 9, 2016, at 4:44 PM, Jaslene Lin <jasle...@hotmail.com> wrote:

Dear Stan developers:

I have made changed to my model which made a huge improvement in terms of the time of simulating and reducing the number of divergent transitions after warmup. However, occasionally, my model can still get divergent transitions after warmup between 1-3, however, if I re-run the simulation again, it might not have divergent transitions. Hence, to get a non-divergent simulation results, I might need to run multiple times, I am wondering is this normal? In all cases, my adapt-acceptance is nearly 1, 0.99999999999. I am not sure whether setting an extremely high adapt_acceptance rate and occasional divergent runs would indicate there is still some problems in my model. Thanks for your insights and explanations.


Kindest regards,
Jaslene
